subject: Critical Thinking
title: Statistical Reasoning: Numbers as Evidence
description: A quick, practical guide to Statistical Reasoning: Numbers as Evidence.

hook.text: '9 out of 10 dentists recommend...' Recommend what? Compared to what? Asked how? Statistics need context.

buildup.text: Statistical reasoning is formalized induction — drawing conclusions from numerical data.

discovery.text: Good statistical reasoning asks: sample size? Selection bias? Confounding variables? Margin of error?

twist.text: 'Correlation does not imply causation' is the most important sentence in statistics. Ice cream doesn't cause drowning.

climax.text: Most misleading statistics aren't wrong — they're presented without the context needed to interpret them.

punchline.text: Numbers don't lie. But they omit very strategically.

quiz.question: What does 'correlation does not imply causation' mean?
options: Two things occurring together doesn't prove one causes the other

details.summary: Statistical reasoning uses numerical data and probability to evaluate claims, distinguishing genuine patterns from random noise. It bridges logic and empirical evidence, providing tools for evidence-based decision-making.
details.whyItMatters: Modern life is saturated with statistical claims, and most people lack the training to evaluate them, making statistical literacy a critical thinking necessity.
takeaways: Sample size and selection methods determine reliability
Base rate neglect is one of the most common statistical errors

faq.question: Why does correlation not prove causation?
faq.answer: Two variables can correlate because of a shared cause, reverse causation, or pure coincidence. Only controlled experiments or rigorous causal analysis can establish causation.

faq.question: What is base rate neglect and why is it important?
faq.answer: Base rate neglect is ignoring how common something is before interpreting new evidence. A positive test for a rare disease is probably a false alarm if the disease is extremely uncommon.
